subject: different detection mode, song and call vs. flush, meadowlark,

messages.author: a5f60541db566238
messages.subject: different detection mode, song and call vs. flush, meadowlark,
parts:
Dear List,
I am trying to obtain density estimates for wintering meadowlarks
(Sturnella magna)in grasslands. When collecting data, I also recorded the
mode of detection (flush, song, or call)(These birds do sing even in
winter, and vocalizations can often be heard from 200 or more meters
away). Regardless of truncation distance, intervals, or model, I was not
able to get any reasonable fit to the data (probability of greater chi-
square value was below 0.000). However, when I fit a model to data from
flushed birds only, I was able to get a reasonable fit (probability of
greater chi-square value ~0.40). Most (~75% of my detections are from
flushes, and most (also ~75%) of my vocalization detections are further
from the line, near 100m or so. Normal truncation distance is around 140
meters regardless of which data sets are used.

What I am thinking of doing is ignoring singing and calls and using
density estimates from the flush data only. I have good sample size even
without using vocalizations, and using flushes only should avoid potential
bias that may arise if the sexes vocalize at different rates. My question
is, if all else were equal (including vocalization rates between sexes)
would excluding one type of detection from my data affect my density
estimates and how? For the record, I don't feel it would because all birds
should have an equal probability of being flushed (equal detection
probability).


I have a feeling I've seen similar discussions in the archives, but have
had no luck in re-finding them. If you are aware of any, please just point
me in the right direction and sorry for the trouble.

Thank you for any help you can give.

Sincerely,
Joe Roberts
Department of Zoology
Univ. of Oklahoma
